Then [T +S] γ β = [T ] γ β +[S]γ β and [cT ] γ β = c[T ]γ β. Proof. Use linearity of T, S, ϕβ, ϕγ to verify. Corollary 5.2. L(V, W ) ∼= Mm×n(F ) under the map T ↦→ [T ] γ β. In particular, dim L(V, W ) = (dim V )(dim W ). Proof. Show injectivity and surjectivity of the map T ↦→ [T ] γ β using β and γ are bases. Definition 5.3. Let A ∈ Mm×n(F ) and B ∈ Mn×p(F ). Then the matrix multiplica- tion C = AB ∈ Mm×p(F ) is given by cij = n∑ k=1 aikbkj. The i-th row, j-th column of C is given by multiplying the i-th row of A and j-th column of B. Proposition 5.4 (Matrix multiplication is composition of linear transformation). Let T : V → W and S : W → U be linear transformations, and β, γ and δ are bases of V, W, U respectively. Then [ST ] δ β = [S] δ γ [T ]γ β. Proof. We write [S]δ γ = (aij) ∈ Mm×n(F ) and [T ]γ β = (bij) ∈ Mn×p(F ) and β = (v1, . . . , vp), γ = (w1, . . . , wn) and δ = (u1, . . . , um). Then ST (vj) =S ( n∑ k=1 bkjwk ) = n∑ k=1 bkjS(wk) = n∑ k=1 bkj m∑ i=1 aikui = m∑ i=1 ( n∑ k=1 aikbkj ) ui. Thus [ST ] γ β = (cij) where cij = ∑n k=1 aikbkj. We can translate definitions and results about linear transformations into matrices. 24 Definition 5.5. For A ∈ Mm×n(F ), we define LA : F n → F m to be the linear trans- formation LA(x) = Ax. (We sometimes do not distinguish A and LA.) The following notation are inherited from those of linear transformations ker A = ker LA, null A = null LA, im A = im LA, rank A = rank LA. The following properties of matrix multiplication follows directly from Proposition 5.4 and Proposition 4.2 applied to LA, LB, LC. Proposition 5.6 (Matrix algebra rules). For any matrices of compatible sizes and any scalar a ∈ F : (i) A(BC) = (AB)C (ii) A(B + C) = AB + AC (iii) (A + B)C = AC + BC (iv) a(BC) = (aB)C = B(aC) (iv) AIn = A, ImA = A The following rank nullity theorem for matrix follows from applying Corollary 4.14 to LA. Theorem 5.7. Let A ∈ Mm×n(F ). Then n = rank A + null A. Definition 5.8. A matrix A is called invertible if LA is invertible. By Corollary 4.11, if A is invertible, then A is a square matrix. By Corollary 4.16, we have the following invertiblity criterion. Corollary 5.9. Let A ∈ Mn×n(F ). The following are equivalent. (i) A is invertible. (ii) null A = 0. (iii) rank A = n. (iv) There is B ∈ Mn×n(F ) such that AB = I. (v) There is B ∈ Mn×n(F ) such that BA = I. If any of the above holds, then the matrix B in (iv) (v) are the same and unique. Definition 5.10. If A is invertible, then the B in (iv), (v) above are called the inverse matrix of A denoted by A−1. Corollary 5.11. Let T : V → W be a linear transformation, β be a basis of V and γ be a basis of W . Then T is invertible if and only if [T ] γ β is invertible. Furthermore, [T −1] β γ = ([T ] γ β) −1. Proof. If T is invertible, then I = [idV ] β β = [T −1T ]β β = [T −1] β γ [T ] γ β. Then [T ] γ β is invertible and we have ([T ]γ β)−1 = [T −1] β γ . If A = [T ]γ β is invertible, then since ϕγT ϕ −1 β = LA, we have T = ϕ−1 γ LAϕβ. Since the right hand side are all invertible, we have T is invertible by Lemma 4.12. 25 5.2 Change of basis formula Lemma 5.12. Let β = (v1, . . . , vn) and γ = (w1, . . . , wn) be two bases of V . Let P = (pij) = [id]γ β ∈ Mn×n(F ). Then vj = ∑m i=1 pijwi for 1 ≤ j ≤ n and for any v ∈ V , [v]γ = P [v]β. Proof. This is a direct consequence of Theorem 4.22 with T = id. Definition 5.13. The change of coordinates matrix from β-coordinates to γ-coordinates is the matrix P = (pij) ∈ Mn×n(F ) such that [v]γ = P [v]β for any v ∈ V . In other words, P = [id] γ β = ([v1]γ, . . . , [vn]γ). The matrix P is also called the change of basis matrix (transition matrix) from γ to β in view of the property vj = ∑n i=1 pijwi for any 1 ≤ j ≤ n. . Remark 5.14. We note here that if P is the change of basis matrix from γ to β, then it is the change of coordinates matrix from β-coordinates to γ-coordinates. The role of β and γ are switched when we switch our view point from change of basis to change of coordinates. Remark 5.15. We also note difference between the definition of change of basis ma- trix, vj = ∑m i=1 pijwi and the usual definition of a matrix A multiplying a vector x,∑n j=1 aijxj. In the first case, the first index of the matrix P is summed over with wj which is a vector, while in the second case, the second index of the matrix A is summed over with xj which is a component of a vector. This is why some people will write (v1, . . . , vn) = (w1, . . . , wn)P for the change of basis matrix thought of as the “row vector” (w1, . . . , wn) multiplying the matrix P in the usual way. Lemma 5.16. Let P = [id] γ β be the change of basis matrix from γ to β. Then P is invertible and P −1 = [id] β γ is the change of basis matrix from β to γ. Proof. Since id is invertible and id−1 = id, by Corollary 5.11 we have P = [id]γ β is invertible and P −1 = [id] β γ . Example 5.17. Let β be the standard basis of F 3 and γ = ((1, 0, 0)t, (1, 1, 0)t, (1, 1, 1)t), then the change of basis matrix from β to γ is [id]β γ =  1 1 1 0 1 1 0 0 1  . In other words, w1 = v1, w2 = v1 + v2, w3 = v1 + v2 + v3. To find the inverse matrix, we have v1 = w1, v2 = w2 − v1 = w2 − w1, v3 = w3 − v1 − v2 = w3 − w2. Then [id] γ β =   1 −1 0 0 1 −1 0 0 1  . Theorem 5.18. Let T : V → W be a linear transformation, β, β′ be bases of V and γ, γ′ be bases of W . Suppose A = [T ] γ β, B = [T ] γ′ β′, P = [idV ] β β′ and Q = [idW ]γ γ′. Then we have B = Q −1AP. 26 Proof. By Proposition 5.4, B = [T ]γ′ β′ = [id] γ′ γ [T ]γ β[id] β β′ = Q−1AP . Corollary 5.19. Let T : V → V be a linear transformation and β ,β′ be two bases of V . Suppose A = [T ]β β, B = [T ]β′ β′ and P = [id]β β′ is the change of basis matrix from β to β′. Then B = P −1AP. Definition 5.20. Given A, B ∈ Mn×n(F ), we say that A and B are similar if there is P ∈ Mn×n(F ) invertible such that B = P −1AP . Finding the simplest matrix which is similar to a given A ∈ Mn×n(F ) is the main reason to introduce eigenvalues and eigenvectors which will be discussed later in the notes. However, if one allows different bases of V and W as in Theorem 5.18, then we have the following theorem. Theorem 5.21. Let T : V → W be a linear transformation. Then there exists a basis β of V and a basis γ of W such that [T ] γ β = ( Ir 0 0 0 ) , where r = rank T . In particular, the rank is the only invariant of a linear transformation under change of basis on both the domain and the target. In matrix language, for any A ∈ Mm×n(F ), then there exist invertible matrices P ∈ Mn×n(F ) and Q ∈ Mm×m(F ) such that Q−1AP = ( Ir 0 0 0 ) . Proof. Let v1, . . . , vn be a basis of V . Then im T = span(T (v1), . . . , T (vn)). By Lemma 2.11, (T (v1), . . . , T (vn)) contains a basis of im T which after relabeling the indices, we as- sume to be T (v1), . . . , T (vr) for r = rank T . In particular, T (v1), . . . , T (vr) is linearly in- dependent. By Corollary 2.16, we can extend it to be γ = (T (v1), . . . , T (vr), wr+1, . . . , wm) which is a basis of W . Since span(T (v1), . . . , T (vr)) = im T , there exist aij ∈ F for 1 ≤ i ≤ r and r + 1 ≤ j ≤ n such that T (vj) = ∑r i=1 aijT (vi). We define ej = vj − ∑r i=1 aijvi for r + 1 ≤ j ≤ n. Apply Lemma 2.12 to er+1, . . . , en one at a time, we see that β = (v1, . . . , vr, er+1, . . . , en) is a basis of V . By definition of ej, we have T (ej) = 0 for r +1 ≤ j ≤ n. Then under the basis β and γ, we have [T ] γ β = ( Ir 0 0 0 ) . 5.3 Dual space Definition 5.22. A linear function (linear functional/ 1-form/covector) on V is a linear transformation φ : V → F . The dual space V ∗ of V is the set of all linear functions on V . In other words V ∗ = L(V, F ). In particular, V ∗ is a vector space. The natural pairing ⟨·, ·⟩ : V ∗ × V → F is defined as ⟨φ, x⟩ := φ(x) for x ∈ V, φ ∈ V ∗. Remark 5.23. In quantum mechanics, a linear function is also called a bra-vector denoted by ⟨φ| while a usual vector is a ket-vector denoted by |ψ⟩. To pair them, just write them together ⟨φ|ψ⟩ and it becomes a “bracket” which is the combined word of bra and ket. 27 Remark 5.24. When we don’t have an inner product on a vector space, e.g. for vector spaces over finite fields, the natural paring serves as an “inner product”. This is why we write it the same way as an inner product. Example 5.25. For V = F n, every linear functional φ : F n → F is given by φ      x1 x2 ... xn      = (a1, . . . , an)      x1 x2 ... xn      = a1x1 + · · · + anxn. for some row vector (a1, . . . , an) ∈ M1×n(F ). Thus (F n)∗ the space of row vectors while F n is the space of column vectors. Definition 5.26. Given a basis β = (v1, . . . , vn) of V , the dual basis β∗ = (φ1, . . . , φn) of V ∗ is defined by φi(vj) = δij for 1 ≤ i, j ≤ n. By Lemma 4.21, φi is uniquely determined by its value at a basis. Proposition 5.27. The dual basis is a basis of V ∗. In particular, dim V ∗ = dim V . Proof. Let φ1, . . . , φn be the dual basis of β = (v1, . . . , vn). We first show that φ1, . . . , φn is linearly independent. Suppose a1φ1 + · · · + anφn = 0. We evaluate both sides on vi for 1 ≤ i ≤ n and get a1φ1(vi) + · · · + anφn(vi) = 0. Since φi(vj) = δij, we have ai = 0 for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n. Hence φ1, . . . , φn is linearly independent. Next we show that span(φ1, . . . , φn) = V ∗. Let φ ∈ V ∗. For any v ∈ V with [v]β = (x1, . . . , xn)t, we have φi(v) = xi for 1 ≤ i ≤ n. We write a1 = φ(v1), . . . , an = φ(vn). Then by Lemma 4.21, φ(v) = a1x1 + · · · + anxn = a1φ1(v) + · · · + anφn(v) = (a1φ1+· · ·+anφn)(v). Since this is true for any v ∈ V we have φ = a1φ1+· · ·+anφn. Remark 5.28. From the proof above, we see that the coordinates of v under the basis β is given by ϕβ(v) = (φ1(v), . . . , φn(v))t. 5.4 Transpose of a linear transformation Definition 5.29. Let T : V → W be a linear transformation. We define the transpose map (dual map/pull-back) T t : W ∗ → V ∗ as T t(φ) = φ ◦ T . That is, for any φ ∈ V ∗ and v ∈ V , (T t(φ))(v) = φ(T (v)) or ⟨T tφ, v⟩ = ⟨φ, T v⟩. Since T t(φ) = φ ◦ T , T t(φ) is a linear function on V since it is a composition of linear transformations. The map T t is linear due to the algebraic rules of composition by linear transformations in Proposition 4.2. Proposition 5.30. Let T : V → W be a linear transformation. Let β = (v1, . . . , vn) be a basis of V and γ = (w1, . . . , wm) be a basis of W . Let β∗ be the dual basis of β and γ∗ be the dual basis of γ. Then [T t] β∗ γ∗ = ([T ] γ β)t. 28 Proof. Let γ∗ = (ψ1, . . . , ψm) be the dual basis of γ and [T ] γ β = (aij). We want to find the coordinates of T t(ψi) under β∗ = (φ1, . . . , φn), the dual basis of β. Let v ∈ V and v = x1v1 + · · · + xnvn. Note that xi = φi(v). Then we have T t(ψi)(v) = ψi(T (v)) = ψi( ∑m k=1( ∑n j=1 akjxj)wk) = ∑n j=1 aijxj = ∑n j=1 aijφj(v) = (∑n j=1 aijφj)(v). Thus T t(ψi) = ∑n j=1 aijφj. That is [T t(ψi)]γ∗ =    ai1 ... ain   . Hence [T t]β∗ γ∗ = ([T ]γ β)t. 29
